LEARNING PATH LESSON · SIGHT WORDS · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Blue — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

Five minutes, one card: you will flap your blue butterfly arms and fly to something blue, and your child will meet “blue” in a real sentence, “The sky is blue.” By the end, “blue” should be a word they know at a glance.

What is this?

“Blue” is a colour word. On this card, a bright blue butterfly with its wings spread wide, with the word printed in big, clear letters underneath.

What does it mean?

“Blue” names a colour, as in “The sky is blue.”

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs to recognise “blue” at a glance, say it clearly, and begin to hear it in the stories you read together. Good hunting grounds: the sky, jeans, toothbrushes and the sea.

Why this matters

Colour words like “blue” are one of the easiest first sight words because the card, the crayon and the real world all agree.

What it teaches

Colour naming, matching the printed word to the real thing and first-letter awareness.

Words to learn

wordcolourcrayon

Say this to your child

“Look at this card. It says ‘blue’. The sky is blue. Now you say ‘blue’. Well done!”

Step by step

  1. Show the card and read “blue” clearly, running your finger under the letters. Let your child say it back, twice.
  2. Look at the picture together: a bright blue butterfly with its wings spread wide. Ask what is happening, then link the picture to the word.
  3. Play one tiny game: flap your blue butterfly arms and fly to something blue. Read the word one last time and stop while it is still fun.

Look closer at the picture

Point to the word first, then to the picture. Cover the picture with your hand and read the word; lift your hand to check. Then let your child trace the first letter with one finger.

Ask your child

“What does the card say?” “What colour is that?” “Can you find something blue in the room?” — answered with a read-aloud, a point and a treasure hunt.

What your child can say or do

Expect a colour-hunting phase: your child may announce “blue” things at the table, on the road and at bath time.

Out in the real world

Watch for “blue” here: the sky, jeans, toothbrushes and the sea. Every sighting is a free practice round: point, say it, move on.

Try it together

Flap your blue butterfly arms and fly to something blue. Finish by saying “blue” one more time.

Understanding check

Tomorrow, hold up the card without saying a word. If your child reads “blue” straight away, the word has arrived; if not, play the game once more and try again the day after.

Parent tips

Always read “blue” in a sentence as well as alone, so your child learns what the word does, not only how it looks.

This lesson pairs with the Blue flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Sight Words (Class 29).
